units: Shared this on Instagram with a photo from my old Olympus: "Shot on a 1974 camera I bought for $20. The light leak in the corner was an accident. My grandfather's hand in the frame wasn't: he was waving me off, and I'm glad I pressed the shutter anyway." Could you tell me what you make of it?

Week 10 of my marathon block, aiming for 3:15. Mon: rest, 15 minutes of yoga. Tue: 8x400 m at 5k pace, 90 s jog. Wed: 10 km easy plus 6 strides. Thu: 16 km with 8 km at marathon pace (4:37/km). Fri: rest. Sat: 8 km easy, then 30 minutes of single-leg RDLs and calf raises. Sun: 30 km, last 5 at goal pace. About 85 km total. Would you change anything?

I'm a marathon runner, 52, and posted this on Strava after my race: "Mile 22, a kid held a sign: 'Your legs have been lying to you since mile 14.' I laughed so hard I forgot to hurt for almost a minute. 4:12. A personal best at 52. Legs are liars. Be a better liar." Does it read okay to someone who doesn't run? Thanks!

I'm a nursing student, and I was asked to say a few words for Carol, a night-shift nurse retiring after 38 years: "Carol taught me that 3 a.m. is when patients tell the truth. Hold the hand, she said, lower the lights, and wait. Thirty-eight years of waiting with strangers so they weren't alone. I may never be as good, but I'll be awake, and that was the first thing she taught me." Honest opinion?

I'm a geologist, and I wrote a book for my niece. "Every stone on the beach was waiting to become something. Dot only wanted to be thrown once, and touch the water seven times." She is, and she does, and then she sinks, slowly, to where the sand is made. Last page: a new beach. Would you give me your honest reaction?

I'm 63, been farming all my life, never given a speech. Tomorrow at the co-op I'll say: "Each of us owns a combine that sits idle 340 days a year. That's eleven machines, eleven loans, eleven rusting evenings. Buy one together and we each keep our money and lose only our pride. And my father's pride never once made a payment." Would that move you if you were sitting in the room?

I'm 16 and run a mowing business with 14 customers. June plan: 14 × 4 visits × $35 = $1,960. Gas $86, trimmer line and blades $30, mower fund $150, flyers $20, tax set-aside 15% ($294), car savings $700, college $380, spending money $300. Zero left over. Mind giving me your honest opinion?

I do community theater as a hobby, and our stage manager Gloria is retiring after 19 years. I'm giving the speech: "Gloria has called 'Places' to this company a thousand times. No audience ever learned her name, which is exactly how she wanted it. Every perfect blackout was hers. So tonight, Gloria, we call it for you. Places, everyone. Thank you. Lights down, applause up." How does it read to you?

I write songs and shared two lines on Instagram: "Mom kept the porch light on like it owed her something / I came home at midnight, paying it back in sorry." They're from a song about leaving my hometown at 19 and coming back at 31. I'm nervous about sharing unfinished stuff. What do you think of these lines?

units: I'm a pipe welder and writing a resume for the first time in about 15 years, so I'm a little nervous. This is what I put for my last job: "Qualified in 6G pipe welding (GTAW root, SMAW fill); passed X-ray inspection on 212 of 214 joints during a refinery turnaround, the highest first-pass rate on a crew of 18." Does it work?

I'm a hospice chaplain, and I've been writing a novel about a family after a death. The first line is: "Grief is mostly logistics, my aunt told me, and then she handed me the casserole dishes and a list of forty-three people to call." I'd be interested in your thoughts.

I'm a junior marketer with an idea I'm nervous to pitch. What do you think of this email to my manager?
"Hi Sam, our unsubscribe page is a dead end: 38% of unsubscribers open it, then leave. Let me test a 'pause for 30 days' option plus a one-question survey. Two-week A/B test, no budget. If it doesn't cut unsubscribes by 10%, I'll drop it. Can I show you a mockup Monday?"

I'm a mycology student making a logo for our research group. A mushroom is seen from underneath in a single deep brown, with its gills radiating out from the stem. The gills are drawn as fingerprint ridges, so the whole cap looks like a thumbprint. The group name is set in small capitals around the edge in a circle. How does it read to you?
I'm 10 and I made up a joke for my class talent show. What did the clock say when it got sent to the principal? "I was only tocking." My mum says I should ask someone else. What do you think?

I'm 19 and write stories in my notes app on the bus. Here's the start of one, I'm kind of curious what you'd say: "My brother says the moon follows our car because it's lonely. I say it follows because Dad drives slow. Either way, by the time we reached Aunt Dee's, it had parked itself over the chicken coop, and the whole backseat had agreed not to mention that Mom was crying."

I'm an occupational therapist, and this is my layout for a sensory garden in a dementia care home. A looped path, 1.5m wide, with no dead ends, so no one gets stuck. Along it, five stations: scent (lavender, rosemary), touch (lamb's ear, grasses), sound (bamboo, wind chimes), taste (raspberries, mint) and a familiar-memory corner with a washing line and a shed. Handrails run along the edges, and the seating is every 12m. Would you give me your thoughts?

I own a tiny used bookstore and we're raising money after a pipe burst. Here's how the letter opens: "Eleven hundred books drowned on a Thursday. I know the number because I counted them as I carried them out, the way you count anything you're about to grieve. Here is what's left: the shelves, the cat, and a hope that you'll help us reopen." I'd love your opinion.

I make candles in my kitchen and I'm trying out new names: "Inbox Zero" (unscented, for the dream), "Sunday Scaries" (lavender, with an undertone of Monday), and "Ex's Sweater" (cedar, regrettably cozy). Which of the descriptions works best, and would you buy any?

I garden as a hobby and wrote this for my friends' wedding: "To graft an apple tree, you cut two different trees and bind them so tightly they forget which wound is which. The scar is the strongest part. Elena grew up by the sea and Marco on a mountain, and by any sane rule they shouldn't have taken. But look at the orchard. To Elena and Marco: may your scar be your best branch."

units:
Hello, I'm a linguist and I wrote this edit distance function for comparing dialect spellings. It only keeps one row in memory:
```python
def levenshtein(a, b):
    prev = range(len(b) + 1)
    for i, ca in enumerate(a, 1):
        cur = [i]
        for j, cb in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur.append(min(prev[j] + 1, cur[j-1] + 1, prev[j-1] + (ca != cb)))
        prev = cur
    return prev[-1]
```
Could you give me your opinion?

I'm a college sophomore and baked these for my floor. Brown butter miso cookies: brown 170g butter, chill until solid. Cream with 100g dark brown sugar, 50g white sugar, 1 tbsp white miso. Add 1 egg plus 1 yolk, 1 tsp vanilla, 220g flour, ½ tsp baking soda, ½ tsp salt. Fold in 150g chopped 70% chocolate. Rest dough 36 hours, bake at 180°C for 11 minutes, flaky salt on top. Honest thoughts on the recipe?

Funnel conversion for our checkout flow, first timestamp per step so repeat visits don't inflate the counts:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'view') AS v,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'cart') AS c,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'pay') AS p
  FROM funnel_events GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT COUNT(v) AS viewed, COUNT(c) FILTER (WHERE c >= v) AS carted, COUNT(p) FILTER (WHERE p >= c AND c >= v) AS paid FROM s;
Casual question: how does it look?

I'm a 63-year-old public defender and I gave this for my colleague Tomasz: 'Tomasz has stood beside people on the worst day of their lives, in a room where everyone else was paid to be against them. He's lost more than he's won. He'd tell you that's the job. He'd also tell you nobody he represented ever stood alone. Counsel rests.' Please tell me what you think.

I drive long-haul and write on the notes app at truck stops. This one came to me in Nebraska. What's your take?
Nebraska takes an hour to finish a sentence.
The grain elevators raise their one white word
and drop it behind me.
Somewhere past Kearney I say your name
to the windshield, which holds it a mile and lets go.

I'm a pediatric nurse and I wrote this for my patients. Opening: "The machine by Tomás's bed made three sounds. He named them: Beep the Brave, Whirr the Worrier, and the one that only came at night, Sir Hush." Over the book he makes friends with each. Could you tell me what you think? I'm a little nervous showing it to anyone.

My grandson says I should share this with someone. I'm 77 and worked as a railway signalman. Logline: "In 1887 Montana, a Chinese laundryman is the only witness to a lynching and the one man the law won't let testify, so he decides to bring the court to his laundry." What are your thoughts?

I'm in an MFA program and workshopping this next week. Before I do, I'd like a fresh reader's take, especially on the line breaks:
The heron holds the river's one idea
so still the water starts to doubt itself.
Then the small bright argument
of a minnow, and the whole grey sentence
resolves into a throat.

I make a local-history podcast as a hobby and want to include it on my resume for a museum education job. Bullet: "Produce a monthly local-history podcast (38 episodes, ~2,500 downloads each); recorded oral histories with 22 longtime residents, three now archived by the county library." What's your opinion?

I design board games as a hobby and I'm giving a talk at a small convention. I'm opening with: "The most important rule in my game is on the back of the box, in small type: 'The player who is winning may not know it.'" What's your opinion?

units:
I'm a mechanic, 52, and my daughter says I should show somebody this. So here goes. Tell me what you think.
Under the hood the engine's cooled to a tick,
a metal clock winding down its day.
I wipe my hands on a rag that's been
every color of every car I've loved.

Nursing student here, running on fumes. I wrote this for our class group chat: "You can tell the week of the semester by the coffee. Week one: oat-milk latte. Week ten: whatever's in the pot. Week fifteen: chewing the beans and calling it 'dry brew.'" Would you change anything?
I started a pest control business last year. For the truck wrap I came up with: "Your house, minus the roommates you didn't pick." Any thoughts on it?

I'm 71 and I knit blankets to sell at the craft fair. My granddaughter told me to ask people online for opinions. This is my tag:
"Merino cot blanket, knitted in honeycomb stitch, which holds warmth without weight. Washed in lanolin so it stays soft. Nine evenings of work. Machine washable on the wool cycle, and made to be handed down: the edges are bound twice, because babies are hard on everything."
Does it work?

I'm a junior copywriter, and this is my first pitch to a real client, a family-owned hearing-aid clinic. My line: "Hear the kettle again. The rain. Your granddaughter's whisper." Nervous to show it. How does it come across?

I run a small ferry and whale-watching business. Captain Joan retires this weekend, and I'll say: "Joan has crossed this bay nine thousand times and still points at the water like she's never seen it. Tourists come for whales. They stay because she makes them look. Joan, you taught us the sea isn't a show, it's a conversation. Fair winds. Your chair stays at the wheel, facing out." What do you think?

I'm a tenant rights lawyer and my firm is Threshold. The mark is a small house silhouette sitting on a long horizontal line. Below the line, the house's reflection is not a house but a key: the roof becomes the key's bow, the chimney becomes one of its teeth. Charcoal above the line, brass below it. I'd appreciate your honest view.

Nursing student here, about to put this on my profile. Can you tell me what you think?
Good at: finding a vein first try, parallel parking, remembering your dog's name.
Working on: sourdough, leaving the group chat on read, believing me when I say "I'm fine."
Night rotations mean my weekends are Tuesdays. If you can be cheerful about dinner at 8 a.m., we'll get along.

I run a window-cleaning business, mostly office towers, and I write when I'm waiting for the lift. Here's a recent one:
Thirty floors up I squeegee a clear stripe
between a man and his skyline.
He doesn't look up.
I wave anyway,
one wet second of me, passing.
Could you give me some feedback?

units: I run a tiny café and I'm testing a new morning bun. Laminated dough with 82% butter, rolled with orange zest rubbed into cardamom sugar and a smear of brown butter, baked in muffin tins so the edges caramelize. Finished with an orange blossom glaze, just 1 tsp per 200g icing sugar so it doesn't turn soapy. Would you put this on your menu? Please be straight with me.

Okay, birders, here's my idea. Lots of us can't describe a song in words, so the app lets you tap the rhythm on the screen and draw the pitch as a rising or falling line. It narrows species by pattern, then plays three candidate recordings to compare. It would also work offline in the field. I'd really like an opinion before I try to prototype it.

Written during a nap I did not get to finish. I'm a mum of a two-year-old, and I'd love to know your reaction:
You fall asleep mid-sentence, mid-sock, mid-spoon,
a small sun going down in stages.
I carry you the way you'd carry soup,
all of me arranged around not spilling.

I run a ten-rod allotment plot and have worked out a four-year rotation. It's divided into four 5x6m blocks: legumes, brassicas, roots, then alliums with potatoes. Between the blocks run 45cm paths that line up with a central compost bay of three bins. Perennials (rhubarb, asparagus, artichokes) sit along the north edge so they never shade anything. Flowers for the bees run along the paths' edges. How does it look to you?

Maths club president, 15. I'm opening the next meeting with this and want a second opinion. "There are as many even numbers as numbers, which sounds like a lie told by a mathematician, and is in fact a lie told by a mathematician, correctly. Pair 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6. Nobody's left over. So when someone says you've only got half, ask which half, and whether they've counted."

Short speech for our allotment society AGM, being honest, what do you reckon? "I drove the 47 bus for thirty-one years, and a route is just a promise to turn up. Allotments are the same. Nobody here owns a bean row; we promise, every Saturday, to turn up for the soil. So when Margaret's marrows win again, remember: the soil won. Margaret just showed up."

I'm a 29-year-old climber working toward my first 8a. Mon: 4 max hangs on a 20mm edge (10 s, +5 kg), then limit bouldering. Tue: 40-minute zone-2 bike, core. Wed: rest. Thu: 4x4s on routes two grades below my limit. Fri: push-ups, reverse wrist curls, shoulder external rotation. Sat: project attempts while fresh. Sun: rest. Every fourth week I halve the volume. How does it look to you?

Just finished the product page for my wallets. Here's the main text: "The Slim Fold. Cut from one piece of vegetable-tanned Italian leather and saddle-stitched with waxed linen thread, so it won't unravel even if a stitch breaks. Holds six cards and folded bills. It starts stiff, then darkens to honey and later coffee as you carry it. In ten years it'll look better than it does today." Honest opinion?

I'm a civil engineering technician and I'm planning a mini concrete project for my niece. We'll cast 12 beams (4x4x16 cm) with 0, 1%, 2%, and 3% fibers by volume (hair, straw, or shredded plastic bags). Each beam is supported at both ends, and a bucket on the middle slowly fills with sand until the beam breaks. The failure load is divided by the beam's mass. All beams will cure 28 days. Does this seem like a solid project?

Learning about the observer pattern at uni, so I wrote my own emitter. Tell me what you think, please!
```js
const emitter = () => {
  const subs = new Map();
  return {
    on(t, f) {
      (subs.get(t) ?? subs.set(t, new Set()).get(t)).add(f);
      return () => subs.get(t).delete(f);
    },
    emit(t, ...a) { subs.get(t)?.forEach(f => f(...a)); },
  };
};
```

units: I run a tiny karaoke bar in Manila and I've been turning my regulars into a script. Logline: "Every Thursday for eleven years, a stranger has sung the same ballad at a karaoke bar; when he stops coming, the tone-deaf owner learns the song and sets out to find him." Thoughts?

Hi! I'm 16 and this is the first logline I've written for a film project in my media class: "When her father, a small-town marching band director, slowly loses his hearing, a teenage drum major secretly conducts the band from the field while he believes he's still leading it." Could you tell me what you think?

I'm 16 and speaking to city council on Tuesday about Sunday library hours. My ending: "Closing on Sundays saves $9,000 a year. But the kid in my building with no wifi still has homework due Monday. The savings show up in your budget. The cost shows up in his grade. Please don't make him pay it." Does this work for a three-minute speech?

Our bakery chalkboard and website need a line for the bread everyone asks about. This is what I wrote: "Sourdough Boule, 900 g. Thirty-six-hour ferment, stone-ground Ontario wheat, a crust that crackles under your thumb and a crumb open enough to hold butter in pools. Baked Tuesday to Saturday, gone by noon. Reserve yours the night before." Can you tell me what you think?

I run a tiny secondhand bookshop, and I've started a magical realist novel. Opening line: "In Santa Ilaria it rained upward on the day my grandmother was born, and for ninety years she never let anyone forget she'd been a weather event first and a baby second." What do you think?

Here's the central question of my philosophy dissertation: "If moral testimony is epistemically legitimate in some domains, what explains why deferring to an expert about whether to donate seems acceptable while deferring about whether to forgive does not?" I'd appreciate your feedback.

I'm a grad student, writing a short story about my grandmother. Sharing the first paragraph with some nerves: "The telegram came on a Tuesday, which my grandmother held against Tuesdays for the rest of her life. She forgave the postman, the war, and eventually God. But Tuesdays she kept, the way a dog keeps a bone, and so for sixty years, every week, we ate cold supper and did not answer the door." What do you think?

I'm a court stenographer who writes thrillers on the side, and I've been sitting on this logline for months. "A court stenographer realizes the defendant's testimony matches, word for word, the transcript of a trial that has not happened yet." Could you give me your opinion?

I'm 81 and this is the first poem I've ever shown anyone. My granddaughter set up this chat for me. I'd be glad to hear what you think.
At eighty I price the stairs by breath:
the fourth one costs a nickel,
the ninth, a dime.
I reach the landing, solvent still,
and spend what's left on the window.

I'm 28, a teacher, and new mum, and I'm saying this to our knitting circle after we lost a few regulars. Feeling a bit emotional about it. How does it read? "A dropped stitch is invisible for six rows, and then it's all you can see. Same with a friend who stops coming. If you're missing someone from this circle, don't wait six rows. Pick up the phone. Pick up the stitch."

units: I own a pottery studio, and people always ask when their pieces come out of the kiln. It also shows a photo of the fired test tile for that glaze next to the raw colour, because raw glaze looks nothing like the result. What's your opinion?

I'm 71 and my doctor mentioned osteopenia. Mon/Thu: 50 heel drops, step-ups in a 5 kg weighted vest, farmer carries with 8 kg. Tue/Sat: 45-minute brisk hill walk. Wed: tai chi class, plus one-minute single-leg stands while brushing my teeth. Fri: band rows, wall push-ups moving toward counter push-ups. Sun: gardening. I add 1 kg to the vest each month. I'd love to hear what you make of it.

I coach a running club and I'm writing my first screenplay. Logline: "A blind marathoner's guide runner begins to lose his own sight, and neither man tells the other." I'm a bit nervous putting it out there. What's your take?

I own a tiny bookshop and tweeted this today: "A customer wanted 'a book that feels like a rainy Sunday but isn't sad.' I hesitated for four full seconds, which is a long time in bookselling, then handed her Howl's Moving Castle. She's back for the sequel and brought her sister." Thoughts?

My small city yard is 15x30 ft, so I made a four-bed rotation plan: Bed A brassicas, Bed B legumes and peas, Bed C tomatoes, peppers and basil, Bed D roots and alliums. Each moves one bed clockwise every year, and compost goes on whichever bed is next to host the tomatoes. Cover crop of crimson clover fills any gap in winter. A 2 ft path loop keeps everything within arm's reach. Opinions?

I'm Nigerian, studying in Leeds, and this is my party jollof. Blend roasted red peppers, tomatoes, scotch bonnet and onion, then fry the base in oil for about 25 minutes until it separates. Add thyme, curry powder, bay and stock. Parboiled rice, sealed with foil under the lid, finishing on low so the bottom catches lightly. Butter at the end. How does the method read to you?

I'm a nursing student and wrote this for my evidence-based practice course. "Among night-shift med-surg nurses, does a protected 20-minute nap at 3 a.m. reduce medication-administration near-misses in the final three hours of the shift, compared with no scheduled break?" Could you give me your honest opinion? I'm a little nervous about it.

I own a flower shop and I'm training for my first marathon (week 10 of 16). Mon: rest. Tue: 8 miles easy. Wed: 6 miles with 3x1 mile at tempo. Thu: 5 easy plus strides, 20 min strength. Fri: rest. Sat: 16 mile long run, last 3 at goal pace. Sun: 4 recovery miles. Wedding season hits in May, so Fridays stay empty on purpose. What's your take?

I'm a herbalist who wants to build a 6m x 6m tea and medicine garden. It's a mandala, with four quadrants divided by paths: calming (chamomile, lemon balm, lavender), digestive (peppermint, fennel, calendula), immune (echinacea, elderberry, thyme), and a quadrant for rotating annuals. In the center, a small sundial surrounded by holy basil. Drying racks are on the shed's south wall. What do you make of it?

units: I'm the only doctor at a rural clinic and I wrote this to open our defibrillator campaign: "Dear friend, The nearest hospital to Dunmore is 61 miles away. The average ambulance takes 74 minutes. I know because I've timed them. Our clinic can do a great deal in the first 74 minutes. It just needs a defibrillator, and a town that knows how to use one." Thoughts?

I'm 16 and run a mowing business with 14 customers. June plan: 14 × 4 visits × $35 = $1,960. Gas $86, trimmer line and blades $30, mower fund $150, flyers $20, tax set-aside 15% ($294), car savings $700, college $380, spending money $300. Zero left over. Mind giving me your honest opinion?

I dispatch buses and write short emails. This one's for my manager. Opinion?
"Hi Pat, route 14's 7:40 is always 8 minutes late because the school crossing on Elm adds traffic. Drivers have logged it for three weeks. Move the timetable to 7:48 and the complaint calls stop. It costs nothing. Thanks, Ruth."

I'm a wedding photographer, and this is a pitch email to a couple choosing between me and a cheaper option: "You'll forget the centerpieces and the playlist. In forty years, you'll want your grandmother's hands adjusting your veil, and your father's face a second before he walks you down the aisle. I take only twelve weddings a year, so I can be standing where those moments happen." Should I send it?

I'm studying literature and tried a folktale. "Tortoise Carries the News." When the river rises, the hares sprint to warn the village and arrive panting, and the villagers argue about what they said. Tortoise arrives hours later and says it once, calmly. Everyone's already packing, because he described every cracked bank he passed on the way. Does the ending earn its moral, in your view?

I'm a 24-year-old ballet dancer, rehearsing six days a week, so cross-training can't add leg fatigue. Mon: 10 minutes of pre-class glute band work. Tue: Pilates reformer. Wed: upper body only, push-ups and rows, 3x10. Thu: slow single-leg calf raises 3x15, tibialis raises. Fri: nothing. Sat: 20 minutes of easy bike. Sun: complete rest, no stretching. Would you change anything?

Funnel conversion for our checkout flow, first timestamp per step so repeat visits don't inflate the counts:
WITH s AS (
  SELECT user_id,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'view') AS v,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'cart') AS c,
    MIN(ts) FILTER (WHERE step = 'pay') AS p
  FROM funnel_events GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT COUNT(v) AS viewed, COUNT(c) FILTER (WHERE c >= v) AS carted, COUNT(p) FILTER (WHERE p >= c AND c >= v) AS paid FROM s;
Casual question: how does it look?

I'm a lifelong birder, and I've designed an app called Quiet List. You record a bird call and it identifies the species and adds it to your life list with a timestamp. For threatened species it saves your location only as a 10 km square, and it never uploads the exact spot. That way nesting sites stay safe, and your data still helps researchers. How does it sound to you?

Just a casual one: I teach myself screenwriting on YouTube and wrote this logline. "In 1889, a widowed schoolteacher enters the Oklahoma Land Run on a borrowed mule, carrying her husband's ashes and a map she has just realized he forged." Thoughts? Anything you'd change?

I own a small print shop and needed delivery dates that skip weekends and holidays. This is what I came up with. Thoughts?
```python
from datetime import timedelta
def add_business_days(start, n, holidays=frozenset()):
    step = 1 if n >= 0 else -1
    d = start
    while n:
        d += timedelta(days=step)
        if d.weekday() < 5 and d not in holidays:
            n -= step
    return d
```

units:
I'm a dad who started making wooden toys on weekends. Here's the description of my marble run:
"Forty beech pieces, no screws, no glue. Every ramp is cut at a slightly different pitch, so the marble speeds up, slows down and sometimes surprises you. Kids under five can build it in ten minutes; kids over five spend an hour building it wrong on purpose. Sanded smooth, finished in food-safe oil."
What do you think?

Hi! For my landscape studio course I designed a 12x20 ft Tucson courtyard. One desert willow in the northwest corner shades the hot afternoon wall. A dry-wash path of granite fines curves through brittlebush, Parry's penstemon and a single blue agave. A rain chain empties into a sunken basin planted with sedges. Seating sits on the east side for cool mornings. No turf. I present Thursday, so what's your take?

I'm trying out new material at an open mic next week and I'm a bit nervous. The bit: "My ex was a cartographer. He said I was distorted at the edges. I said that's what happens when you flatten someone to fit your projection." Could you tell me how it reads?

I analyze my own online chess games for fun. Here's how I score my openings as Black, counting draws as half a point and ignoring openings I've played fewer than 20 times:
SELECT opening, COUNT(*) AS games,
  ROUND(AVG(CASE result WHEN 'win' THEN 1.0 WHEN 'draw' THEN 0.5 ELSE 0 END), 3) AS score
FROM games
WHERE color = 'black'
GROUP BY opening
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20
ORDER BY score DESC;
What do you reckon?

For my environmental science class I'm talking about my own town. I wrote: "My town's creek has flooded four times in my lifetime. My grandfather's 1962 map shows exactly where the water would go, and we built there anyway." Could I get your thoughts on it as an opening?

I'm launching a green burial company called Return. The symbol is a single leaf, outlined, whose veins branch out in the closed concentric whorls of a fingerprint, so the leaf also reads as a human thumbprint. Deep moss green, slightly uneven line, like it was pressed in ink. Name below in a quiet serif. I'm hoping you can give me an honest response.

I run a small bakery and wrote this to scale recipes by flour weight. What do you think?
```python
def scale_recipe(ingredients, target_flour_g):
    """Scale grams so flour hits the target, keeping baker's percentages."""
    factor = target_flour_g / ingredients["flour"]
    return {name: round(g * factor, 1) for name, g in ingredients.items()}
```

I run a tiny bakery and posted this on our Instagram story at 8:45 this morning: "Sold out of croissants by 8:40 again. To the man who asked if we'd make more: we would, but the butter has a schedule and so do I. Tomorrow's batch goes in at 5. Come at 7 and you'll have a croissant. Come at 9 and you'll have a story." Too cheeky? Let me know!

My project: how does plate thickness affect Chladni patterns? I'll vibrate square aluminium plates (1, 1.5, 2 mm) with a speaker driver and sweep frequency until sand forms the same mode shape. Theory predicts frequency scales with thickness, so I'll plot f against t and see how close my data comes. I'll photograph each pattern. Does this seem like a good plan to you?

I'm 68 and retired, and my main goal is staying steady on my feet for gardening and grandkids. Mon: 20 min walk, sit-to-stand 3x10, heel-to-toe walking. Tue: resistance bands, upper body. Wed: tai chi class. Thu: walk plus single-leg stands near the counter. Fri: light dumbbell work. Sat: garden (counts!). Sun: rest. Does this seem like a reasonable week to you?

units: I'm an amateur astronomer and posted this on Facebook: "Saturn tonight through my $90 telescope: tiny, tilted, impossible, rings like a hat. My daughter asked if it was a sticker on the lens. I said no. She was quiet for a full minute, which has never happened." Tell me what you think!

Here's my hellstrip plan, 8x25 ft, Ontario zone 5, casual and just for fun. Three height bands. Front: prairie dropseed at 18 in spacing, so it reads tidy to neighbours. Middle: golden alexanders, then pale purple coneflower, then anise hyssop for a May to September bloom run. Back: New England aster and little bluestem for October colour. Seedheads stay up until March for the finches. What would you change, if anything?

First-year law student. I told my study group: "The 'reasonable person' is the only one in law school who's never late, never confused, and has always done the reading." Everyone groaned in a good way, I think. What do you make of it?

I sell empanadas from a food truck and I'm writing the market manager. I'm excited but a bit nervous:
"Hi Ms. Lindqvist, I've been at the Saturday market for 14 weeks and sold out by 1 p.m. every time. Could I move from the back lot to the corner near the fountain? The line currently blocks no one, but at the corner I could double the queue space. I'd also add a compostable-packaging pledge. Happy to chat. Warmly, Valentina"

I'm a volunteer firefighter and this is my pitch for a side business: "We sell rural fire departments a $4,000-a-year subscription that replaces paper pre-incident plans with drone-mapped 3D layouts of every farm, so crews know where the anhydrous ammonia tank and the old propane shed are before the truck arrives." Be honest, what's your take?

I'm a divorce lawyer, and I write romance on the side under a pen name. Here's my opening line: "The custody agreement gave Dev the house and Priya the sourdough starter, and neither of them, in the end, knew how to keep the thing alive." How does it read to you?

I'm a freelance designer and invoice clients in installments. This shows what each client still owes. I aggregated billed and paid separately first so the joins don't multiply rows:
WITH b AS (SELECT client_id, SUM(amount) AS billed FROM invoices GROUP BY 1),
p AS (SELECT i.client_id, SUM(pay.amount) AS paid FROM payments pay JOIN invoices i ON i.id = pay.invoice_id GROUP BY 1)
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(b.billed, 0) - COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS owed
FROM clients c LEFT JOIN b ON b.client_id = c.id LEFT JOIN p ON p.client_id = c.id
ORDER BY owed DESC;
Thoughts?

I'm an undergrad writing my history honours thesis. My question is: "Why did Ottoman port authorities in Salonica begin recording ship cargoes in French in the 1880s, and what does that choice reveal about who the records were meant for?" What's your opinion?

I run a small bakery and I'm mentoring a student with this idea. Sourdough starter in identical clear jars, same flour and hydration, held at 18, 22, 26 and 30°C in water baths. Time-lapse photos mark rise height every 10 minutes. Then we compute peak-rise time and estimate Q10 for fermentation. Three jars per temperature. How would you rate the approach?

I wrote this for my little brother, whose dad works nights. "The House Is Wearing Its Quiet." Every afternoon Theo tiptoes through the rooms like they're a sleeping animal: cereal without crunching, cartoons on captions only. At four o'clock Dad's alarm rings, and the whole house exhales and gets loud again. How does it read to you? Be straight with me.

units: I'm 65 and just retired after 40 years as a high school band director. At my party I said: 'Forty years of teenagers, and I've heard every wrong note a human can play. I miss none of them. I miss all of them. Please don't clap on one and three. And if you must cry, do it in tempo.' Casually curious how that works on paper.

I'm a backend developer applying to a food bank's tech team, taking a pay cut to do it. Cover letter paragraph: "Last year I rewrote our checkout retry logic and saved my company an estimated $2M. This year I'd like to spend my skills on a problem where success is a Tuesday pantry line that moves twelve minutes faster. Your volunteer scheduler has a race condition. I found it in ten minutes and would love to fix it." How does it land?

I'm 71 and my doctor mentioned osteopenia. Mon/Thu: 50 heel drops, step-ups in a 5 kg weighted vest, farmer carries with 8 kg. Tue/Sat: 45-minute brisk hill walk. Wed: tai chi class, plus one-minute single-leg stands while brushing my teeth. Fri: band rows, wall push-ups moving toward counter push-ups. Sun: gardening. I add 1 kg to the vest each month. I'd love to hear what you make of it.

I run a weekend food truck and this is my birria. Short rib and goat shoulder, 2:1. Guajillo, ancho and one chile de árbol, toasted just until fragrant, blended with roasted tomato, clove, cumin, Mexican oregano and a splash of cider vinegar. Braise 3.5 hours at 160°C. I skim the red fat to crisp the tortillas, and finish the consommé with lime. What would you change, if anything?

I'm a baker, so I'm up at 4am anyway. My cafe opens at 6:30 for the people on early shifts: bus drivers, midwives, cleaners. It's called "Half Past." You'd say, "Meet me at half past," and everybody knows it's an easy hour to get to. Just wondering what comes to mind when you read the name.

I'm a stay-at-home dad and write a little blog for family and friends. Newest post: "My Son Narrates His Own Life and I Am Taking Notes." First line: "At four, Theo describes every action in the third person, 'Theo is putting on the sock, the sock is reluctant,' and I have started to suspect he's the only one of us paying attention." What do you make of it?

I'm a PhD student and this is the first tweet of a thread I'm about to post: "Tardigrades survive the vacuum of space. Mine did not survive a long weekend in our lab cabinet. A thread on how they actually do it (a protein called Dsup shields their DNA) and why 'indestructible' is the wrong word. 1/" Should I change anything before I hit send?

Librarian here, please tell me what you think of my bio: "Things I can find: your lost book, the quietest chair in any building, a good reason to stay in. Things I can't: my keys, a gym habit. I've read two thousand novels and still don't understand people, which is why I'd like to keep studying one. The reference desk is open."

I'm studying literature and tried a folktale. "Tortoise Carries the News." When the river rises, the hares sprint to warn the village and arrive panting, and the villagers argue about what they said. Tortoise arrives hours later and says it once, calmly. Everyone's already packing, because he described every cracked bank he passed on the way. Does the ending earn its moral, in your view?

I'm nervous about this one. It's my first design: a 10x10 ft moss garden under a Japanese maple in Portland. A single weathered basalt boulder sits off-centre, with raked gravel flowing around it like a stream. Hair cap moss goes on the shaded side and cushion moss on the sunlit side. A slate stepping path bends once so you can't see the whole garden at a glance. Would you tell me what you think?

units:
I'm new to selling tea and a little nervous. Here's the description I wrote for one of my teas:
"Lapsang Souchong, smoked over pine. A campfire in a cold cabin: resinous, faintly sweet, with a surprising hint of dried longan on the finish. Steep at 95°C for three minutes. Try it with salty cheese, or with rain."
Could you tell me how it reads?

Film studies sophomore, and I'm excited about this paper. Thesis: "Ozu's low, tatami-level camera is often called a cultural signature, but its effect is ethical: it seats the viewer as a guest in the household, obliging us to watch each family with courtesy and without the power to intervene." What's your opinion?

I'm a chef and I've been asked to speak at a food conference, which feels odd because I usually just cook. My opening: "Salt is the only rock we eat on purpose, and for ten thousand years we've argued about which ones taste best." What do you think?

I'm a hospice chaplain, and I've been writing a novel about a family after a death. The first line is: "Grief is mostly logistics, my aunt told me, and then she handed me the casserole dishes and a list of forty-three people to call." I'd be interested in your thoughts.

I own a laundromat, and my customers inspired a song, so here's the chorus. English is my second language, so I'm curious how the words sound to you. What do you think?
Spin cycle, spin cycle, the whole block's laundry turning,
I learned my English at the folding tables here.
Every lonely sock, I keep in a box by the door.
Someone always comes back, if you wait a year.

I'm 24, a line cook, and this is the first real budget I've made. $2,700 a month: rent 850 (roommates); groceries 220 (staff meals help); transit 127; phone 45; loan minimum 190; credit card payoff 300; savings 400; fun 250; gym 30; new knives fund 60; cushion 228. I'd love an honest opinion. Please be gentle!

I track my D&D group's attendance. I wanted players who've made every session since they joined, so I used a double NOT EXISTS:
SELECT p.name
FROM players p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM sessions s
  WHERE s.played_on >= p.joined_on
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1 FROM attendance a
      WHERE a.session_id = s.id AND a.player_id = p.id));
This is my first time trying that. Does it work for you?

I coordinate a women's shelter and this is the opening of our winter appeal: "Dear friend, The first thing most women ask for when they arrive isn't food or a bed. It's a key, to a door that locks from the inside. We have eight keys. Last year we turned away sixty-three women." I'd really value your opinion before I send it.

units: I'm a marine engineer starting a sailboat rigging business, Bowline Marine. The mark is a rope tied in a bowline, drawn as one thick line in navy. The loop of the knot forms the bowl of a capital B, and the standing part runs down as its stem. The working end of the rope tucks behind, and you can follow the knot correctly. Does it hold up, in your view?

I'm a retired electrician, 68, starting a blog. Title: "The Last Man in Ohio Who Still Respects Knob-and-Tube Wiring." First sentence: "In 1931 somebody in Zanesville ran two wires through a wall using porcelain tubes and a prayer, and I have spent forty years learning to respect that prayer." Be straight with me, what's your honest reaction?

Public speaking terrifies me, so I kept mine short. Whole toast: "I met Sam in a lift that got stuck for forty minutes. By minute ten we'd stopped being strangers. By minute forty I'd have happily been stuck anywhere with him. Jo, you've had longer than forty minutes. I hope they've felt like ten. Cheers." Is short okay for a best man's speech?

Pastry chef here, testing this for our autumn menu. Pear and rye tart: rye flour pâte sucrée, filled with brown butter frangipane (120g butter, browned and cooled; 120g almond flour; 100g sugar; 2 eggs). Fan thin slices of roasted Bosc pear on top, then glaze with thyme-infused honey and finish with flaky salt. Bake at 175°C for 38 minutes. I'd love an outside opinion before it goes on the menu.

I coach marathoners. My app is called Negative Split. Most pacing apps talk constantly, which drives me nuts. This one stays silent while you're within 5 seconds per mile of target. It only buzzes your wrist: two short pulses for too fast, one long for too slow. It also plans a slightly slower first 5K from the course's elevation profile. Can you give me feedback?

Retired court stenographer here, age 71. I've started on a screenplay, and this is my logline: "A 911 dispatcher takes a call from a woman who only whispers about her cat, and has eleven minutes to decode what the cat means before her abuser returns." I'd love an outside opinion, if you don't mind.

I'm a college sophomore starting a laundry fund for students who can't afford the machines. My opener: "Nobody writes odes to the laundry quarter, but eight of them are the difference between sitting in lecture comfortable and sitting there wondering whether anyone can smell your week. We'd like to make that difference free." Opinion?

I'm a sci-fi nerd and I run a small comic shop. Here's my movie logline: "A janitor aboard a generation ship discovers that the destination planet was reached two hundred years ago, and the officers have been circling in secret because they like being officers." What do you think?

Pitching my D&D group on the next campaign: "You're all accountants to the villains. Nobody swings a sword. Every fireball comes with an invoice, the dragon's hoard needs an audit, and the Dark Lord will be furious about Q3. Trust me, the most terrifying thing in any dungeon is a well-organized ledger." Would this get you to say yes, or should I tone down the absurdity?

Proposal to my team to kill our "smart suggestions" feature. Key paragraph: "Suggestions are used by 3% of users and generate 31% of our support tickets. Every feature is a promise to maintain it forever. We aren't deleting a feature; we're refusing a lifelong loan with a 3% return. Cut it, and move those two engineers to search, which 90% of users touch daily." Sending it Monday. Any thoughts first?

units: Nursing student here, working on a startup idea for my entrepreneurship elective. The pitch: "Night-shift nurses lose about twenty minutes per shift re-explaining patients at handoff, so we turn a 90-second spoken summary into a structured SBAR note that the incoming nurse approves with one tap." What's your opinion?

I run a tiny bakery and posted this on our Instagram story at 8:45 this morning: "Sold out of croissants by 8:40 again. To the man who asked if we'd make more: we would, but the butter has a schedule and so do I. Tomorrow's batch goes in at 5. Come at 7 and you'll have a croissant. Come at 9 and you'll have a story." Too cheeky? Let me know!

I'm a pipe welder and writing a resume for the first time in about 15 years, so I'm a little nervous. This is what I put for my last job: "Qualified in 6G pipe welding (GTAW root, SMAW fill); passed X-ray inspection on 212 of 214 joints during a refinery turnaround, the highest first-pass rate on a crew of 18." Does it work?

I own a small bike shop and wanted to test something instead of guessing. The question: "Among first-time commuter bike buyers, do those given a free 30-day tune-up return for paid service within a year at higher rates than those given 10% off accessories?" I'd assign the offers by purchase week. What's your opinion?

I'm 24, self-taught, applying to illustrate for a children's publisher. Paragraph from my letter: "My portfolio has no dragons. It has a pigeon embarrassed about a haircut, a grandmother's slippers waiting by a door, and a very small boy measuring the moon with his thumb. Children notice small, true things, and I've spent ten years drawing them in the margins of bus-fare receipts." Any thoughts?

No stove in my dorm, only a rice cooker, so here's what I make: ½ cup jasmine rice, 6 cups water, 3 slices ginger and one dried shiitake on the porridge setting. Ladle the boiling congee over a bowl of raw minced scallion, ginger and salt so the heat wilts them. Top with a soft egg, soy, white pepper and chili crisp. Is this a decent recipe? Be honest!

I came to the UK ten years ago and posted this on Facebook today: "Ten years ago I arrived in Leeds with two suitcases and one English word: sorry. Today I fixed the boiler of the woman at the bus stop who taught me the second: thanks. She paid in scones. I accept this as legal tender." English is my second language, so I'd love your opinion on how it reads.

Freelance illustrator, income swings a lot. I budget off my lowest month of the last year, $2,400: rent 900; food 320; health insurance 210; phone/internet 90; software 55; transit 60; personal 125; tax account 640. Anything above that gets split: 30% tax, 40% buffer until I hit three months, 30% to me. Thoughts? Be blunt.

I'm a potter and wrote this between kiln loads. Chip is a mug with a cracked lip who gets hidden when guests come. During a power cut, small hands choose him, because the chip fits a thumb exactly. The last line: "Perfect is for looking at. Chip is for holding." I'm unsure whether to keep that ending as written. What would you do with it?

I'm a college junior and I've been writing a coming-of-age novel about a boxing gym. Here's the first line: "The summer I turned sixteen I learned two things about my father's gym: that it smelled of liniment and forgiveness, and that nobody ever came there to win." Could you give me feedback?

units: I'm a dog groomer and I've been wanting to write for my clients. Title: "Your Dog Is Not Afraid of the Bath." First sentence: "Most dogs I meet aren't afraid of water; they're afraid of slipping, and once you put down a rubber mat, the 'bath-hating' dog you've described for six years quietly disappears." What's your take?

I translate novels for a living, and I wrote a haiku about the part of the job that never makes it into interviews:
Last line of the book—
I leave one word as it was
like a light left on
How does it read to you? Any lines you'd question?

I do woodworking as a hobby and have started writing haiku in my shop notebook. Here's one. I'd love your opinion!
Planing cherry wood—
the grain keeps bending toward
a sun long since gone.

I'm opening a cafe that serves coffee by day and natural wine by night. I'd name it "Zenith & Nadir," the highest and lowest points, one for each half of the day. I'd value hearing what you think of it.

Fifty-three, in marketing for 25 years, and updating my resume for the first time in a decade. One bullet: "Rebuilt the email onboarding flow for a B2B SaaS product, A/B testing 14 variants; trial-to-paid conversion rose from 8.2% to 13.5%, adding $1.1M in ARR." Would love to hear what you make of it.

I run a small bakery and wrote this haiku during a 4 a.m. shift:
Flour dusts my wrists—
the oven ticks, half awake,
before the first bird.
Could you tell me what you think of it?

Paralegal here, trying to move into litigation support. I'd love a second pair of eyes on this bullet: "Built a privilege-log template and tagging protocol that cut document review for a 400,000-page antitrust production from an estimated 9 weeks to 5, with zero clawback requests." What's your take?

I'm an amateur astronomer, and my brother asked me for a toast. "When you look at a star, you're seeing light that left it long ago. Some of those stars are gone by the time you notice them. I think of that when I look at Hana and Theo, because what I see tonight, two people lit from inside, started years ago, in a lab hallway, over a broken coffee machine. Keep shining across the distance. To Hana and Theo." Does that read as natural?

I'm putting this on my dog-grooming flyer: "Your dog can't tell you his ears hurt. He can only shake his head and look at you. A groomer sees mats, ticks, and lumps weeks before a vet appointment would. Book every six weeks and you get a clean dog and a second set of eyes." Does the tone feel right to you?

I'm opening a vet clinic called Tailwind. The mark is a dog's tail, side-on, drawn as three nested arcs of decreasing length, each stroke a bit thinner. They read as a wag, but they also read as wind lines. The clinic name sits to the right in lowercase, and the arcs are teal. I'd love a candid reaction before I send it to the printer.

Where would you push on it?

I'll fold 5 identical planes for each wing design (none, up, down, and split tips), throw each one 10 times, and record the glide distance from a fixed height. Then I'll calculate the glide ratio for each. Does this sound good to you?

units: I run a tiny bookkeeping firm and wrote this for our newsletter: "Bookkeeping is archaeology for people who hate dust. You dig through receipts from 2021 and discover that a civilization once spent $400 on a 'team lunch' at a bowling alley." Does it work, or should I cut it?

I'm an accountant, 58, and this is my first Toastmasters speech. Terrified. "I spent my career making columns agree. Zero is the most honest number I know; it never pretends. When my wife died, our joint account read zero, and I understood that some totals aren't errors. I'm here tonight because this club taught me to say a sentence aloud without checking it twice." Any feedback welcome.

Our daughter cried when the snow melted, so I wrote this on my lunch breaks. "Snowman, Stored." Odile hides her snowman in the chest freezer between the peas and Dad's fish, visiting daily with a scarf. By July he's the size of a grapefruit. In December she introduces him to the first snowfall like a returning relative. I'm a plumber, not an author. Thoughts?

I'm a high school senior applying for a front-desk job at a vet clinic. Here's my paragraph, and I'd like to know your opinion, even if it's blunt.
"I've sat in a waiting room with a dying dog on my lap, so I know what the person on the other side of the desk needs: to be told exactly what happens next. I'm good with forms and phones. But I'm best at saying, quietly, 'Take all the time you need.'"

I've played jazz piano for thirty years but only recently started writing my own lyrics. Here's a ballad chorus:
The moon is a borrowed coat tonight
Too wide in the shoulders, it still smells of you
I wear it down the avenue
Pretending that it's mine, pretending that it's new
I'd value your impressions.

Posting this for a workshop at my community college. It's the opening of a dystopian story: "On the day the oceans were rationed, my mother taught me to cry efficiently: one eye at a time, over a bowl, so the salt could be returned. 'Grief is a resource,' she said, wiping my cheek with a measuring spoon. I was seven. I remember thinking that she was very good at it." How does it read to you?

I'm 12 and I wrote a story about a dragon. Here's the beginning, can you tell me what you think?
"The dragon was not asleep. Everyone in Pell assumed it was, because that was easier than the alternative. Every night I carried its supper up the mountain and told it a story, because the one night I forgot, it came down to the village to ask for the ending."

I translate novels for a living, and I wrote a haiku about the part of the job that never makes it into interviews:
Last line of the book—
I leave one word as it was
like a light left on
How does it read to you? Any lines you'd question?

Maths club president, 15. I'm opening the next meeting with this and want a second opinion. "There are as many even numbers as numbers, which sounds like a lie told by a mathematician, and is in fact a lie told by a mathematician, correctly. Pair 1 with 2, 2 with 4, 3 with 6. Nobody's left over. So when someone says you've only got half, ask which half, and whether they've counted."

I teach physics and wrote this over the holidays. Opening paragraph:
"The last astronomer on Earth kept her telescope pointed at the same dead star for forty years, not because she expected it to change but because someone had to be there for the nothing. Her grandson thought this was sad. She thought it was the only job left that was entirely honest."
I'd love to hear what you think.

units: I run a Saturday knitting circle, and we're opening a cafe where each table has a basket of yarn and needles. The name is "Cast On," the first step of any project and an invitation to start something. Does it work for you?

I'm sixteen and I've been writing a fantasy novel in my notebooks all year. Here's the first line: "Every child in Vesk is given a shadow at birth, and mine was returned, politely, with a note saying there had been a mistake." Would you keep reading? Tell me what you honestly think!

I've been gardening for years and finally boiled the experience down: "My tomato plants and I have an understanding. I water them daily, and in return they produce eleven tomatoes, all on the same Tuesday, while I'm out of town." Does it read well to you?

I write narrative for video games and I'm trying prose for the first time. Here's an opening paragraph:
"The map was wrong in the way maps are wrong when they love you: it left out the cliff, the wolves, the long unfashionable middle of the journey, and drew the sea closer than it was. Imre followed it anyway. You can forgive a lot in something that wanted you to arrive."
How does it come across?

Hi! I run a tiny candle shop and rewrote the listing for our bestseller. Here it is: "Low Tide, 8 oz. Smells like the moment after a wave pulls back: wet granite, a thread of sea salt, the faint green of kelp drying in the sun. Hand-poured soy, cotton wick, 40-hour burn. Light it when the weather's wrong and you'd rather be on a beach." What do you think?

I'm a vet, and I want to start a dental plan for pets. $19 a month covers a yearly scaling under anesthesia, a home-brushing kit, and a video call with a tech every quarter to check your technique. I've seen too many dogs lose teeth at eight because the cleaning cost $600 at once. My plan makes that cost small and regular. Be honest, would you sign up your own dog?

I'm a barber, and I'm rolling out "Quiet Chair" on Sunday mornings. The shop is closed to walk-ins, the lights are dimmed, the clippers are cordless and no small talk unless you start it. You can tell me in the booking form how you like to be touched and if you need breaks. It was designed with my autistic nephew. $5 more than a regular cut. Would you book it?

Here's my idea: erosion control. I build four 30° slopes in trays: bare soil, grass, mulch, and gravel. A watering can with 100 drilled holes simulates 20 minutes of steady rain from a fixed height. I collect the runoff and dry it to find the sediment mass, and I measure the total water volume too. Three replicates per cover. What do you think?

Proud of this one from my SQL homework! Find students who've completed every required course:
SELECT s.name
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.completed
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id AND c.required
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM courses WHERE required);
I'd really like your feedback on it.

I roast coffee in my garage and I'm calling the brand Longitude. The logo is one coffee bean in dark espresso brown. The centre crease is a straight meridian line running top to bottom. A tiny dot sits on it, showing the exact spot of my town's coordinates, and the numbers are printed small underneath. Tell me what you think.

units: I'm 72 and my granddaughter doesn't speak Tagalog. So: in Lola's kitchen there's one rule, you can only ask for something by its name in the other language. "Pass the salt" becomes "asin," and soon Mari is hungry in two languages. Every page adds a word and a recipe. What's your opinion? Be honest, I've survived worse.

I own a bike shop, and our mechanic Tomasz retires after 25 years. I'm proud of this one: "Tomasz can hear a loose bearing from across the shop and a lie from across the street. He fixed ten thousand flats and handed back every bike like it was new. Tomasz, we're keeping your bench exactly as it is, greasy thumbprints and all. Nobody's allowed to clean it." Thoughts?

I'm a tailor, and my book is about trousers. "Hem" follows one pair of corduroys across three brothers. Each page the hem is let down an inch, and the pockets hold what the last boy left: a pebble, a bus ticket, a dried worm. On the final page the youngest hears the jingle and realizes he's wearing his brothers' whole childhoods. Tell me what you think!

Proud of this one from my SQL homework! Find students who've completed every required course:
SELECT s.name
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.completed
JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id AND c.required
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM courses WHERE required);
I'd really like your feedback on it.

I own a small bakery and write on slow afternoons. Here's how my short story opens: "The first thing my grandmother taught me about bread was that it lies. 'Dough tells you it's ready when it isn't,' she'd say, 'and tells you it's ruined when it's only shy.' She died in March. I have fed her starter every day since, though it has never once forgiven me for not being her." Honest thoughts?

I'm a night-shift nurse in Phoenix, and I designed a garden I can enjoy at dusk with no lawn. The layout: a decomposed granite courtyard, a central ring of boulders around a palo verde for shade, agave and red yucca on the south edge, and a night-blooming cereus and white evening primrose along the patio. A drip line runs on one timer, three zones. Total water use is under 15% of our old lawn. What's your take?

Nervous about this one! I'm a history major applying for archive internships, and this is my lead bullet: "Transcribed and indexed 312 pages of 1890s ledgers at the county archive, uncovering a pattern of wage withholding at a local cannery that became the basis of my 40-page honors thesis." Could you tell me what you think?

Our running club coach Beth is retiring from teaching, and I volunteered to speak. Draft: "Beth's entire coaching philosophy was one sentence: 'You're not slow, you're early for the next mile.' I've repeated it on hills, in hospital corridors, once outside a divorce lawyer's office. Beth, you never timed us. You just stood at the finish line with a thermos, as if you'd always known we'd arrive." Honest thoughts welcome.

what do u think??

```js
const units = { d: 864e5, h: 36e5, m: 6e4, s: 1e3 };
const toMs = str =>
  [...str.matchAll(/(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*([dhms])/g)]
    .reduce((t, [, n, u]) => t + n * units[u], 0);
```

```js
class LRU {
  #max; #map = new Map();
  constructor(max) { this.#max = max; }
  get(k) {
    if (!this.#map.has(k)) return;
    const v = this.#map.get(k);
    this.#map.delete(k);
    this.#map.set(k, v);
    return v;
  }
  set(k, v) {
    this.#map.delete(k);
    this.#map.set(k, v);
    if (this.#map.size > this.#max)

  }
}
```

units:
Hi! For my databases course I had to list every consecutive-day login streak per user. Here's my Postgres attempt:
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_at::date AS d FROM logins),
g AS (SELECT user_id, d, d - (ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d))::int AS grp FROM d)
SELECT user_id, MIN(d) AS starts, COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM g GROUP BY user_id, grp
ORDER BY streak_days DESC;
What do you think?

I run a small catering business, and our cooking club asked me to talk about salt. "Salt isn't a seasoning. It's a volume knob. Too low and the tomato whispers; too high and it screams. Taste, add, taste again, until the tomato sounds like itself. And salt early: pasta water should taste like a mild sea, not an insult." I'm a bit nervous. Does it work as an opening?

I'm 16, a goalkeeper, and season starts in six weeks. Mon: box jumps 4x4, band-resisted lateral shuffles. Tue: team practice. Wed: pull-ups 4x6, Nordic curls 3x5, Copenhagen planks. Thu: practice, then 10 minutes of tennis-ball reaction catches off a wall. Fri: mobility only. Sat: match. Sun: easy swim, shoulder prehab. Nothing heavy within 48 hours of a match, so I planned around that. Any thoughts? Be straight with me.
I'm a retired sailor who now makes waxed canvas bags. Slogan for the tag: "Carried through worse weather than this." I'd like to hear what you think.

I sell empanadas from a food truck and I'm writing the market manager. I'm excited but a bit nervous:
"Hi Ms. Lindqvist, I've been at the Saturday market for 14 weeks and sold out by 1 p.m. every time. Could I move from the back lot to the corner near the fountain? The line currently blocks no one, but at the corner I could double the queue space. I'd also add a compostable-packaging pledge. Happy to chat. Warmly, Valentina"

I illustrate on commission from my home studio and I'm pitching a children's book publisher. Here's the paragraph from my letter, wondering what you think.
"I draw the sort of picture a child finds on the third reading: the mouse behind the curtain, the half-eaten pear under the bed, the cat who looks guilty in every scene. My sketchbooks are full of these small secrets, and I would like to hide them in your books."

Here's one I've been saving for my chess club's newsletter: "My chess rating is like my houseplants: technically alive, and no one is sure why." I'm pretty nervous about sharing it since some of those guys are brutal. How would you rate it?

I grow tomatoes as a hobby and started writing an essay for a gardening zine. Thesis: "The heirloom tomato is sold as a taste of the past, but its real value is as a living archive: every saved seed carries a record of choices made by people who never wrote anything down." Curious what you think!

I'm a mycology student making a logo for our research group. A mushroom is seen from underneath in a single deep brown, with its gills radiating out from the stem. The gills are drawn as fingerprint ridges, so the whole cap looks like a thumbprint. The group name is set in small capitals around the edge in a circle. How does it read to you?

I own a small bakery and write on slow afternoons. Here's how my short story opens: "The first thing my grandmother taught me about bread was that it lies. 'Dough tells you it's ready when it isn't,' she'd say, 'and tells you it's ruined when it's only shy.' She died in March. I have fed her starter every day since, though it has never once forgiven me for not being her." Honest thoughts?

units: My project compares 3D-printed infill patterns: gyroid, grid, and honeycomb. Each test cube is adjusted to exactly 12.0 g (±0.1) so strength is per unit mass. I print five of each and load them with sand until they fail, recording the mass of sand at the crack. Same filament, same print temperature. Tell me what you think, please. I'm happy to take criticism.

Stand-up comic, 26, and I finally wrote a bio I'm ready to post. "I'm funnier in person, which is the worst thing a comedian can put on a dating app. Five-six, or six if the shoes are loud. I will make a joke about our first fight during our first fight. Looking for someone who can take a punchline and deliver a better one." Be honest!

I'm a retired schoolteacher and volunteer for our branch library. Here's how my fundraising letter opens: "Dear neighbor, In 1952 the Alder Street Library had 3,000 books and one stove. Today it has 11,000 books and the same stove. We are asking you to help us buy a new one, and, while we're at it, a roof." Any thoughts?

I'm a student and wrote a short poem for my Instagram, kind of nervous to ask but what do you think? "My grandmother counts in two languages: / Polish for coins and stairs, / English for the days since Dziadek, / and for the rosary, no language, / only the click of the next bead."

I'm a plumber and I came up with this for the side of my van: "Every house has one pipe that's been quietly holding a grudge since 1974." My wife says it's too long for a van. Be straight with me: would you read it, and would you call me?

This is my first draft for an industrial design class assignment. "Halo Clip is a rear bike light that wraps around the seatpost and glows in a full ring, so drivers see you from the side as well as behind. USB-C charging, 12-hour runtime, and a silicone band that fits any post from 25 to 35 mm. At 41 grams, it weighs less than two AA batteries." Thoughts?

I'm a night-shift nurse and cook when I'm exhausted, so this is a one-pot dinner. Toast 2 tsp cumin seeds in olive oil, add onion, garlic, then 1½ cups red lentils and 6 cups water. Simmer 20 minutes. Stir in the chopped rind of half a preserved lemon, finish with lots of black pepper and a spoon of yogurt. Chili butter on top. Does this sound like something worth making again?

Sorry if this is a bit odd. I work in a post office sorting room and this came to me on shift. The start of my story:
"The dead letter office in Perth received, in 1962, a parcel containing forty-one left shoes. No note, no sender. Winifred Ames, who had spent nineteen years reuniting strangers with their mistakes, laid them in a row on the sorting table and felt, for the first time, outmatched."
What's your take?

Warehouse supervisor, learning SQL at night. Stock upsert that ignores out-of-order updates from the scanners:
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty, updated_at)
VALUES ('A-114', 25, now())
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
SET qty = inventory.qty + EXCLUDED.qty,
    updated_at = EXCLUDED.updated_at
WHERE inventory.updated_at < EXCLUDED.updated_at;
I'd appreciate your opinion. Be gentle, it's my first real one!

Latest reading per sensor, for a dashboard that refreshes every few seconds. I'm an IoT hobbyist with a Raspberry Pi and a lot of sensors:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (sensor_id) sensor_id, recorded_at, temp_c
FROM readings
WHERE recorded_at > now() - interval '1 hour'
ORDER BY sensor_id, recorded_at DESC;
I also have an index on (sensor_id, recorded_at DESC). Any feedback would be great!

units: I'm a dog walker and I'm putting together business cards. The slogan I wrote is "Tired dogs, happy couches." Can you tell me what you think? I'm a bit nervous about showing it to anyone.

I teach piano in a rural village and I'm making a logo for my studio, called Flock Music. Five staff lines roll like green hills. Perched on the lines as notes are little sheep: a round woolly body for the note head and a thin stem upward for the tail. One black sheep is a note in the middle. What do you think of the idea?

I've kept bees for six winters and finally tried to capture the sound in a haiku:
January hive—
I press my ear to the wood
and hear them, still there
What's your take? I'm especially unsure how the last line is read by someone outside beekeeping.

I run a pottery studio and I'm starting a scholarship fund for teens. The letter opens: "Clay doesn't care about your grades. It doesn't care who your parents are, or whether you've eaten today. It only cares whether you're paying attention. We'd like to offer fifteen teenagers a seat at the wheel, free, for a year." How does it read to you?

Flight instructor here, applying to a regional airline. This is the bullet I lead with: "Instructed 47 students to private pilot certificates with a 94% first-attempt checkride pass rate, versus a 71% national average." Curious how it reads to someone outside aviation. Thoughts?

My grandmother actually ran a dry cleaner, which inspired this. "A Korean grandmother who has worked in a Brooklyn dry cleaner for thirty years is the only witness who can identify a killer, but she has spent those years pretending not to speak English." Does this work for you? I'd love to hear your opinion.

i'm 22, barista, write poems on receipts. my bio: "I'll remember your order by the third visit and your name by the fifth. Hoping to be remembered back. Currently reading three books, finishing none. Fluent in sarcasm, conversational in Portuguese. If you like rainy bus rides and arguing about whether cereal is soup, hi." thoughts?

Hey, I coach distance runners and write a small newsletter. Next post is titled "Mile 20 Is a Negotiation." I open with: "Nobody warns you that at mile twenty your body will open with a lowball offer, and the whole skill of the sport is knowing it's only the first one." Could you tell me how this reads to you?

I'm a stay-at-home dad and write a little blog for family and friends. Newest post: "My Son Narrates His Own Life and I Am Taking Notes." First line: "At four, Theo describes every action in the third person, 'Theo is putting on the sock, the sock is reluctant,' and I have started to suspect he's the only one of us paying attention." What do you make of it?

Nervous about sharing this, but here's the thesis for my game design class essay: "Tetris endures not because it is simple but because it is unwinnable: its design turns inevitable failure into a measure of skill, teaching players to take pleasure in managing loss rather than avoiding it." Would love your reaction.

This is the bullet I'm sharing in my cover letter too: "Secured $480K in first-time foundation grants by pitching 23 funders; raised donor retention from 38% to 54% by personally calling every donor who gave over $100." How does it land for you?

I've kept a sourdough starter for four years and decided to write about it. Thesis: "Pandemic sourdough was less a food trend than a time trend: a starter demands feeding on a schedule, and people locked at home wanted something that made the days measurably pass." Any reactions?

I'm a bassist who's been touring for ten years and this has happened to me twice. "When a band's player gets sick the night before a gig, we get a vetted session musician who has already studied their charts and setlist into the van within twelve hours." What do you think?

I'm a beekeeper with six hives, and I planned a 10m x 10m forage garden to support them from March to October. Early: crocus, willow, and hellebores. Spring: lungwort, borage, and fruit blossoms. Summer: lime tree, phacelia, and marjoram. Autumn: ivy, Sedum, and asters. Hives are in the southeast corner, facing away from the path, with a 2m hedge forcing bees to fly up. What do you think of it?

Just graduated and applying for backend jobs. This is the first bullet under my internship: "Reduced p95 checkout API latency from 1.8s to 310ms by replacing N+1 Postgres queries with batched lookups and adding a read-through Redis cache, saving an estimated $42K/yr in compute." What do you think? Anything you'd change?

I run a bike repair shop and I'm finally writing for our website. Title: "Your Bike Isn't Making That Noise to Annoy You." Opening: "Every click, tick, and groan from a bicycle is a tiny confession, and after eleven years of fixing them above a laundromat, I can usually tell you what yours did last weekend before you finish describing the sound." Feedback welcome!

I own a small bike shop and wanted to test something instead of guessing. The question: "Among first-time commuter bike buyers, do those given a free 30-day tune-up return for paid service within a year at higher rates than those given 10% off accessories?" I'd assign the offers by purchase week. What's your opinion?

Hi! I'm a nurse with 12 years in, updating my resume for a unit manager role. Here's my top bullet: "Cut central-line infection rate on a 28-bed cardiac step-down unit from 4.1 to 0.7 per 1,000 line-days in 14 months by redesigning the dressing-change checklist with night-shift staff and training 63 nurses." Can you give me your honest opinion?

Stand-up comic, 26, and I finally wrote a bio I'm ready to post. "I'm funnier in person, which is the worst thing a comedian can put on a dating app. Five-six, or six if the shoes are loud. I will make a joke about our first fight during our first fight. Looking for someone who can take a punchline and deliver a better one." Be honest!

I'm a hobbyist drone photographer and want to pitch a hotel manager. Here's the email:
"Dear Ms. Aoki, I'm a local photographer, and last week at golden hour I shot your hotel's rooftop terrace from above, attached. The frame shows the pool, the hills behind, and the sunset hitting the cabanas. I'd be glad to shoot a full set of ten images for your website for $250. I'm licensed to fly in this area. May I send a quote? Regards, Daniel"
What do you think?

units: I'm a civil engineering technician and I'm planning a mini concrete project for my niece. We'll cast 12 beams (4x4x16 cm) with 0, 1%, 2%, and 3% fibers by volume (hair, straw, or shredded plastic bags). Each beam is supported at both ends, and a bucket on the middle slowly fills with sand until the beam breaks. The failure load is divided by the beam's mass. All beams will cure 28 days. Does this seem like a solid project?

Hi! I'm 16 and this is the first logline I've written for a film project in my media class: "When her father, a small-town marching band director, slowly loses his hearing, a teenage drum major secretly conducts the band from the field while he believes he's still leading it." Could you tell me what you think?

Hobbyist beekeeper here. Our club's oldest member, Arlo, is hanging up his veil. My toast: "Arlo told me bees don't care about your day. Move slow, breathe, and they'll let you in. I've tried to live that way since. Sixty years, millions of bees, and only eleven stings, he claims. Arlo, you kept the hives and the humans calm. We'll leave the smoker lit for you." Do you think it works?

Soup dumplings from scratch, my weekend project. Filling: 500g pork with 30% fat, ginger-scallion water added in three batches and stirred in one direction, then 300g cold pork-skin aspic, cubed and folded in. Wrappers: hot-water dough, rolled thin at the edges and thicker in the centre, 18 pleats. Steam 8 minutes on cabbage leaves. What would you improve?

I'm a line cook who got curious about browning. I'll caramelize identical onion slices in solutions of baking soda at five different pH levels, then photograph each batch every 5 minutes next to a gray card and convert the pixels to L*a*b* color values. Then I'll plot how fast browning happens against pH. I'm a little nervous presenting at a science fair as a non-scientist. What do you think of it?

I've been home with my kids for 8 years and I'm applying for a project coordinator job. Nervous! Paragraph: "For eight years I've managed a team of three with unpredictable deadlines, no budget, and a 6 a.m. launch every day. I also ran the school auction, which raised $41,000 using one spreadsheet and fifty unreliable volunteers. People call that a transferable skill. I'd like to prove it on yours." Honest reaction, please?

I run a pet-sitting business and I'm emailing the manager of the kennel I partner with. Here goes:
"Hi Greta, over July 4th weekend, I'd like to reserve five overflow kennels for my regular clients. All five dogs are vaccinated, and I'll send their records by Friday. I'll drop off, feed, and walk them myself, so there's no extra work for your staff. I can pay $200 up front. Could you confirm by the 20th? Thanks, Marcus"
What do you think?

I'm the groom's boss, and I was asked to speak, which I assume means they ran out of friends. My line: "In six years Hugo has never missed a deadline except one: the Friday he left early to propose. I've never been so glad to be let down. Tess, we got a great employee. You got the rest of him, and I'm told that's the better deal." Thoughts?

Hi! I'm sending this to my manager at the coffee shop tomorrow. Here it is:
"Hi Dana, I have organic chemistry finals May 6 and 9, so I can't do my Thursday closes those weeks. Priya and Marcus both said they'd take them if I cover their Sunday opens on the 12th and 19th. I've already put the swaps in the shared sheet. If anything clashes, I'm happy to rework it. Thanks, Leo"
What do you think?

Long-time fantasy reader, first-time writer here. My novel begins: "Tuesday was the day Thornwick hid its children, so the dragon's tax collector found only goats, a very old man, and an unusually loud silence." Would you tell me what you think? Be gentle, I'm a bit anxious about this.
